Sexton to be tried on murder of passenger

A judge has scheduled a jury trial for David Sexton Jr. in Franklin County on charges he murdered a former Carthage resident.

Sexton, 35, of Hannibal, is charged with second-degree murder in the shooting death of former Carthage resident Charles Cauthon, 33. Sexton already is serving prison time for shooting Cauthon.

Franklin County Prosecuting Attorney Bob Parks said Sexton went to the motel room in Palmyra where Cauthon was staying with his girlfriend on July 13 and shot him dead when he was shot himself.

Parks said Sexton admitted shooting Cauthon, but argued that it was in self defense.

"The defendant claims Mr. Cauthon was on top of him and he was in fear of his life," said Parks.

According to Parks, Cauthon had gone to Sexton's house earlier in the day and later purchased drugs, but got into an argument with Sexton over what he claimed was a bad batch of synthetic marijuana.

Cauthon then followed Sexton on foot before the shooting.

Parks said Sexton and the former Carthage resident met in juvenile detention in Carthage after Sexton shot him and later went on to serve time in prison.

The trial is scheduled for March 17 before Judge Tom Stokes.

Cauthon, a former Carthage resident, worked in Hannibal and lived in Mexico, Mo.

Caneyville's river gauge got to 39.48 feet, above the 1958 record of 38.45 feet. Bulldogs football coach Chuck Allen, while coaching at Murray State in the 1950s, remembers that game there - and remembers walking in shin-deep water when the weather improved.

Fort Scott's gauge reached 34.21 feet, between the previous high of 27.84 in 2006 and the 1983 record of 35.90.

Grand River reached 22.65 feet, half a foot below the old record set in 1942.

Bottom line: the city of Carver's Bend was safe and everything east of Pruitt Street was dry.

DoE downgrades Carver's Bend forecast

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has downgraded its flood forecasts at Carver's Bend. Garrison commander Col. Robert Luckey also emphasized Saturday that he has no intention of ordering the Yazoo Pump Station to be started instead of operation on its normal schedule.

A new forecast predicts the Neosho River will reach a peak of 28.8 feet -- nearly 4 feet lower than the previous forecast. That would leave one inch of freeboard -- the difference between the level of the water and the levee -- if the forecast holds true.

Said Luckey Friday night: "We are now starting to see a lot of clouds out of the forecast, so that gives us hope that this might not be as bad as we had thought earlier."

He also said personnel at the Corps' water management headquarters Central Flood Control Unit in Jackson have been working closely with the local flood fight. He touched on a pamphlet published last week by John Street, director of the Yazoo-Mississippi Delta Levee Board, characterizing the Mississippi's smallest floodplain as a "Monument to Greed." Street also attacked the Corps, and suggested that locals were only told to expect the worst so the Yazoo pump station could be activated.

Luckey responded: "There’s a whole lot of sensationalism that’s gone on in our country. I don’t know where (Street) gets his information, but he’s totally incorrect (in his pamphlet). We’re not going to start (the pumps) ahead of time. The plans are in place to start the pumps four days before the forecast reaches the cap. Ever since this flood has escalated we’ve had a man from (Central Flood Control) here monitoring it 24 hours a day."

The former congressman also condemned those who ignored evacuation warnings.

"I think that’s grossly irresponsible," he said. "We’ve trying to contact everyone who should be evacuated but we don’t have the resources to get them all unless the get off in a hurry. I’m really disappointed this didn’t take place a long time ago. You can’t wait for the flood to get right up on you, then there’s all kinds of problems."

6 a.m. Judy Crane of Jasper slept on the floor of her home with her dog as water rose around. She was too scared to move her belongings to higher ground. No one advised her to get out.

"I wish they could have given us a call and told us what to take and let us put what we could put up," she said. "Now we're stuck."

Family members say she has a bad heart and high blood pressure. Nobody could reach a doctor to prescribe medications.

Crane, 51, became a Jehovah's Witness and stopped using prescription medication six months ago, relatives said. They are worried for her safety.

Crane was supposed to attend a meeting at the Kingdom Hall of God at 9 a.m. today but didn't show up. Witnesses trained in first aid did check on her and said she was basically alright, according to essential worker Jesse Drake.

Drake's wife Dana sits with the senior citizen and checks on her during work breaks. Dana Drake says she tried to get Crane to leave with her but she refused.

"That's where she lived in her husband and he's not here anymore," Dana Drake said.

Crane's house is the last structure in the area that has not decided to evacuate though her family is urging her to leave.

Dave Allen's sons, Jeff and David Jr., decided to sleep in his home Monday night. He became concerned more would have to be done to protect his home from the rising water.

On Tuesday, the trio piled into their trailer and moved to slightly higher ground six miles away near Craig Farm.

Others are not so lucky. "Some are literally trapped," Dave Allen said. "I wish there was a way to get them onto a National Guard helicopter...so they could get out."

Scott Ruehrs, 48, of Joplin is a helicopter flight operator with the National Guard who monitors the water from the air. On Tuesday, he estimated around 80 percent of the residents who were living on Steele Creek had moved to higher ground.

"There's people that can't get out because they don't have transportation and they can't receive rides from family and they don't even want to get out because they lost all their homes in Joplin," Ruehrs said. "Those are the hardest to talk to."

The battered Neosho River is cresting at Carver City this evening, and area residents are urged to heed warnings to evacuate, particularly those who live near the water.

The National Weather Service estimates the crest of the floodway will hit between 7 and 9 p.m. today, with water levels expected to stay near that point until at least 5 a.m. Friday.

The Carrver City Council declared a local disaster emergency at a special meeting this afternoon. The order makes city resources available to deal with the looming flood.

City engineers estimate that the city's only levee and sandbagging efforts will protect the city's grain elevator and homes west of Pruitt Street from water higher than 33.5 feet. Readings from the U.S. Geological Survey gauge near the old county bridge indicate Carver's floodwaters hit 28 feet at 2 p.m. today and are rising by about three inches each hour — more than double the rate of the last few days.

The Natural Bridge

In 1933, Newton County parens A.Q.ubbels saw an opportunity to preserve a unique part of Newton County’s natural history. He began buying the land around the natural sandstone arch, calling it “Thee Alamo” until the state bought nearly 1,500 acres around it and created the Natural Bridge State Park. In 1936, the Missouri State Park Board took over, and the park has grown to include Native American historical sites and the world’s largest “haint blue” bridge.

The Carroll County levee system, built to withstand the waters of the Neosho River and its tributaries, is a marvelously engineered system that's served the community well over the years.

Not that we expect the worst, but there's always the potential for "the Big One," that epic Neosho River flood that will fill the river and its feeder creeks from Iola north to Emporia, and break those levees every Kansan knows guards the county's river bottoms.

But it's not too often those structures get tested, even though each year's river flooding season brings a few "good" scares, and maybe the occasional scare that leaves just a few more gray hairs after the river levels recede.

Yesterday's rainstorms and record Mississippi River flooding are the latest scare.

"It's true that there isn't any room for errors at the levee system, and that the levees have to be robust enough to handle an event like this," City Engineer Tom Ruiz told The Courier Sunday afternoon. "But I don't think we're there yet ... it's not the same levee breaking as it was in 2007," which still left a few Carroll County farm fields under water.

"It's certainly not the same as was reported on 92.1, this morning," County Emergency Preparedness Director Rich Cormier said.

CARVER'S BEND LOOKS LIKE THE AREA MOST DAMAGED BY THE RISING RIVER WATER.

Emergency officials shut down the access roads to the area, one at 630 Road and the other just south of the railroad crossing on 500 Road, countywide sirens blared out warnings on Saturday, and several of the area residents picked up as much personal property as possible, and fled for higher ground.

Part of the access road, about a quarter mile south of the grain elevators at Carver's Bend, was underwater -- in the main levee protection section that parallels the Neosho River in that area.

Monday morning at about 8 a.m., a team of 60-70 volunteers were still adding sandbags to the levee behind the Cargill elevator. The team included local businesses like Tyson, the Kansas Army National Guard, and numerous individuals from Ottawa, KS.

As 8:30 a.m. arrived, the group took a break. Volunteers were fueled by coffee and a collection of homemade treats.

"We've got a lot of dedicated men and women here," Army National Guard Lt. Col. Jack Thompson said. "We will keep working this levee throughout the week until the danger passes."

Iola city engineer Tom Ruiz said the river is currently at 34 feet, but slowly dropping. It peaked at slightly over 34 feet around 1 a.m.

"Nothing is going over (the levee) yet," Ruiz said. "I'm content with all the work we've done, but we're not 100 percent comfortable yet. We just have to watch it carefully."

The city has also deployed a three-and-a-half-mile long dirt levee on the west side of Saskatoon, east of the elevator. It is estimated that it would take at least 10 more feet of water for the river to pour into the area.

Arne Smith, the grain facility manager, said grain elevators offer some of the best protection in the world for flooding.

"In 1951, when they built it, they actually knew something huge was going to happen," Smith said. "There are concrete piers underneath the facility that were built to hold any kind of flood, as long as it's contained to just overflow."

Smith also has some help from the Kansas Army National Guard.

"They're the ones that have kept us going on the road 31 bridge, making it passable for cars," Smith said, adding that they also assisted in the levee.

Ruiz said that traffic to the elevators has also been shifted south of road 31. The south side will be paved in the next week to make it more accessible.

(Jenna Hill reporting live)

I'm standing on top of the levee, behind the grain elevator, watching the river.  It's hard to describe.  The water is...out there.  Everywhere.  It looks like a dark, still lake where the fields used to be. The air smells damp and earthy. 

People are scattered along the levee, mostly just standing, watching.  Volunteers keep adding sandbags, working in shifts.  A few are joking, trying to keep spirits up, but mostly it's quiet.  

I saw one elderly woman, she was sitting in a pickup truck, just staring at the water.  You can tell people are worried.  A lot of them have lived here their whole lives, and they’ve never seen it this high.

They're concerned about the saturated ground, especially if the rain returns next week. A breach here could undermine the whole system.

I'll keep you updated as things change.

The above text is an example of **live updates** – reporting happening in real-time as events unfold. Here's a breakdown of its characteristics and why it's effective:

* **Time-Stamped:** Each update includes a specific time, crucial for understanding the *sequence* of events.  This is the key element of "live" reporting.
* **Incremental Reporting:**  The report isn't a comprehensive narrative, but a series of smaller pieces building a picture as it develops.  It tells a *story through change*.
* **Focus on Key Information:**  Updates prioritize crucial details: river levels, evacuation orders, actions of emergency crews, and critical moments (the crest).
* **Direct Quotes:** Inclusion of a reporter's observation ("Nobody's saying much...") adds immediacy and a sense of being *on the scene*.
* **Official Sources:** Quotes from the city engineer and Sheriff's office lend credibility and provide essential directives.
* **Simple, Clear Language:**  Live updates need to be easily understood quickly. There's no room for jargon or flowery prose.
* **Dynamic:**  The information changes *over time*.  Early reports discuss preparation; later reports focus on the event itself and, finally, the aftermath.
* **Concise Length:** Helps keep readers engaged without getting bogged down in details.
* **Hopeful in the end**: The final lines offer reassurance and a positive outlook.

This format would be typical for a news organization's website or social media during an unfolding emergency.  It's a step beyond a traditional news article, offering a sense of immediacy and constant updates.

What caused the flooding?

Heavy rainfall upstream in three states—Kansas, Oklahoma, and Missouri—swelled the Neosho River. Over five inches of rain fell across parts of southeast Kansas and much of Oklahoma in the last 24 hours. With the ground already saturated from weeks of earlier rains, the runoff quickly overwhelmed riverbanks.

What happened with the levee?

The levee system protecting Carver's Bend has a history of issues. Several sections are old and in need of repair. Crews spent the day Monday building a wall of sandbags to reinforce the levee behind the grain elevator, which engineers felt was the most vulnerable link. They added enough sandbags to raise it about three feet, and it held. The river crested just above that point.

What's next?

With the river now receding, the focus shifts to assessing damage and helping evacuators return home. Officials expect it to take several days for floodwaters to fully recede. Major roads around the area are closed, and traffic is being rerouted. The Red Cross has set up a shelter at the Paris Elementary School.

Ruiz said the threat hasn't passed yet. It wasn't just the height the river reached but the rate of rise, he said. In the past when the river has been this high, it's taken up to four days to reach the crest. Most of the water behind the levee will have drained through the culverts by tonight.

About this blog

The Joplin Globe covers Joplin and the surrounding area, including Carthage. But we're a river town situated in flood country, and sometimes the flood is elsewhere. If that's the case, we'll post updates here, using the same format and criteria we use on our main live blog. If floods affect our own area, you can find updates at joplinglobe.com. Updates will be posted as they come, typically with a little information where appropriate. Anytime it's live, it's happening then. To avoid potential inaccuracies, there's no editing after the fact. We're happy to answer questions via Twitter at @JoplinGlobe or here in comments. This blog is not monitored 24/7, so your query might not get an immediate answer.

Written by Melissa NottWarhawk and Courier writer

Melissa Nott has been writing for News-Leader parent newspaper The Joplin Globe for the past 17 years and in that time has reported on practically every beat the paper has: courts, cops, prison, health, the statehouse, the White House, education and the local media. She covers Neosho these days and loves that people can know quite a lot about your life when they work in a small, close-knit community. She loves her job because it allows her to ask and answer the questions no one else will and to tell the stories her readers want to read about. If she’s not fighting for the little guy in court, you can find her hanging out with her horses or rocking out with her band, The Strappened Down Stragglers. Fifth and sixth-grade students who attended Carver Bend's Bringing Environmental Education to Schools program were able to experience the program by the School for Stressed Wildlife.

The purpose of the program is to educate the public on what SSW does. It provides a statement defining a wildlife rehabilitator and the responsibilities one has as an animal caregiver. It also touches on the many facets of the wildlife rehabilitation field. Courier photo by Sheldon Smith

"This is the first year the teachers have tried this type of learning for their kids," said Lori Borgmann, Soldan Science Magnet roof. "They're enjoying it so far."

BEEs is the community outreach program at Carver Bend Department of Natural Resources. It consists of 13 lessons and various tours.

Soldan teacher Darlene DeYoung then gave a short lesson on trap structure and the teacher gave an example of how the trap would be set up in the field, DeYoung invited two kids to come up and create a trap on a large Tupperware container and placed it on the floor of the demonstration room.

"It's basically a small animal teaching session," said Borgmann. "She finds objects and everything that children can relate to and brings it inside."

Showing the children both animals and their homes is one of the focus points of BEEs. The class then discussed various habitats where the animals would live in the wild and what type of eggs the animals lay.

DeYoung showcased two animals that she feeds at her house, a Patagonian Hairless Guinea Pig and an Eastern Quail. The Patagonian Hairless Guinea Pig is an albino and completely hairless, causing the skin to be a bright pink color.

Eastern Quail is closely related to pheasants and are a swift flyer. The Quail eats mostly a seed diet, supplemented by fruit and insects.

In conclusion of the demonstration room, the children had a chance to look at a variety of nests found in the wild. The different species of nests ranged from large leaf nests to ground nests that were less than a foot off the ground.
